title: Stocking stitch receiving blanket
subtitle: A lightweight square receiving blanket in DK with a garter border.
excerpt: A 90 by 90 cm receiving blanket in DK stocking stitch (US: stockinette) with a 5-stitch garter border on all four sides to prevent curling. About 300 g of machine-washable DK. The square format suits swaddling.
sourceNotes: Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870), §Infants' Knitted Shawl and Receiving Blankets, describes square stocking-stitch receiving blankets with a knitted border as a standard pattern. Weldon's Practical Knitter, 3rd series (1887), §Baby Wraps, notes the need for a garter-stitch edge to prevent the stocking stitch from curling.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 30 rows = 10 × 10 cm in stocking stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: The most common knitted fabric: knit on the right side, purl on the wrong side when working flat. Produces a smooth face of V-shaped stitches. Curls strongly at the edges without a border and must be blocked or bordered to lie flat.

A band of garter stitch (knit every row) worked along all four edges of a stocking-stitch piece. Because garter stitch lies flat of its own accord, the border counteracts the curl tendency of stocking stitch and keeps the blanket flat.

content.text: A single-panel square worked flat in
stocking stitch
(US: stockinette) with a 5-stitch
garter stitch border
on all four edges, finishing at 90 cm square, blocked.

A single panel is washable as one piece without risk of a seam opening. Stocking stitch was chosen over garter for its softer face and lighter drape at this yarn weight; a receiving blanket that lies against a newborn benefits from a smooth, not ridged, surface. The garter borders on all four sides prevent the stocking-stitch body from curling, which it would do aggressively without a border. Budget about 300 g (about 660 m / 720 yards) of machine-washable DK. Buy all the yarn at once in matched dye lots. A square this size is a standard swaddling and tummy-time blanket.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 300 g (about 660 m / 720 yards) of DK-weight machine-washable yarn
items.substitutions: Superwash merino DK or DK cotton for a cooler fabric. Stocking stitch shows yarn quality more than garter; choose a yarn with good stitch definition.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 100 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 30 rows to 10 cm over stocking stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. Take a 15 cm swatch, wash it, pin it flat, let it dry, and measure the centre 10 cm. Stocking stitch opens significantly after wet blocking; the blocked gauge will read 1 to 2 stitches fewer per 10 cm than the unblocked gauge.

If your blocked stitch gauge is 24 per 10 cm with a 208-stitch cast-on, the blanket will be about 86 cm wide. If it is 20 per 10 cm, the width will be about 104 cm. Adjust the cast-on to a multiple of 1 stitch (no repeat required for the body) plus 10 stitches for the two garter borders (5 stitches each side).
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 208 stitches (5 border + 198 body + 5 border). Long-tail tail: (4 × 208) / 10 + 15 = 83.2 + 15 = 98 cm. Measure 110 cm of tail.
Bottom border (5 rows)
Work 5 rows of garter stitch across all 208 stitches (knit every row). This forms the bottom border of the blanket.
Body with side borders
RS row: k5 (garter border), k198 (stocking stitch body), k5 (garter border).
WS row: k5 (garter border), p198 (stocking stitch body), k5 (garter border).
Repeat these two rows until the body section (excluding the bottom and top borders) measures 80 cm from the top of the bottom border. At gauge that is approximately 240 rows of stocking stitch body.
When you set this aside between sessions, a sticky note marking RS or WS is enough to pick it up without error.
Top border (5 rows)
Work 5 rows of garter stitch across all 208 stitches. Cast off knitwise with a relaxed tension.
Stitch count check-ins

At row 135 of the body section (about 45 cm above the bottom border): count across. You should have 208 stitches. At row 268 of the body section (about 89 cm above the bottom border): count again before beginning the top border.
Common faults

Stocking stitch curling at the side edges despite the garter border: the garter border stitches were purled on a WS row instead of knitted. On every WS row the first and last 5 stitches must be knitted, not purled.

Holes or ladders at the garter-to-stocking-stitch transition: tension loosened where the yarn was carried between the border knit stitches and the body purl stitches. Snug the transition stitch slightly on each WS row.

Blanket not lying flat even after blocking: the garter border is too narrow to counteract the stocking stitch's curl at this yarn weight. If this is an issue, increase the border to 7 or 8 stitches on each future blanket.
Blocking

Wet block the finished blanket: soak in cool water for 15 minutes, press in towels to remove most of the water, then lay flat on a blocking mat and pin to 90 cm square. Use about 20 pins along the edges to keep the square true. Leave to dry completely, which takes several hours.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle. Lay flat to dry. The blocked shape returns after each wash so long as the blanket is dried flat. Do not tumble dry.
What to try next

Once the garter-border stocking-stitch panel is comfortable, the same structure can carry a simple textured pattern in the body: a basket-weave or seed-stitch body between the same garter borders. The border count and cast-on stay the same; only the body rows change.
